message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection directly from here, but you can quickly find out your current download/upload speeds with a couple of simple steps:

---

### 1. Use the **speedtest‑cli** command (if you have it installed)

If you already have the `speedtest-cli` Python package (or the standalone binary) installed, you can run:

```bash
speedtest-cli --simple
```

This will print something like:

```
Ping: 12.34 ms
Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
```

If you don’t have it installed, you can add it with:

```bash
pip install speedtest-cli
```

or, on Windows, you can download the executable from the [speedtest‑cli GitHub releases](https://github.com/sivel/speedtest-cli/releases).

---

### 2. Use an online speed‑test website

If you prefer a browser‑based test, just visit one of these sites:

- https://www.speedtest.net/
- https://fast.com/
- https://www.fast.com/ (Netflix’s test)

Click “Go” or “Start” and the page will automatically measure your ping, download, and upload speeds.

---

### 3. Run a quick test from PowerShell (no extra installs)

If you’re on Windows and want a quick test without installing anything, you can use PowerShell to download a file and time it. Here’s a one‑liner that downloads a 10 MB test file from Hetzner and reports the speed:

```powershell
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/10MB.bin"
$client = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
$sw = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
$client.DownloadFile($uri, "$env:TEMP\hetzner_test.bin")
$sw.Stop()
$bytes = (Get-Item "$env:TEMP\hetzner_test.bin").Length
$seconds = $sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes / 1MB) / $seconds
Write-Host ("Download speed: {0:N2} Mbit/s" -f ($mbps * 8))
```

This will give you a rough estimate of your download speed. (Upload speed would need a separate upload test.)

---

#### Want me to try running a command on your machine?

If you’d like me to attempt to run `speedtest-cli --simple` right now, just let me know and I’ll execute it for you.
